title: The Lego Figures Taken Apart
text:
In a study published in 2008, Dan Ariely, Emir Kamenica and Drazen Prelec asked students to assemble small Lego Bionicle figures for money. Each figure paid a little less than the one before, starting at two dollars, and the participant could stop whenever the pay no longer seemed worth the effort.

There were two conditions. In the meaningful condition, every finished figure was placed on the table in front of the participant, and the row of completed models grew as they worked. In the Sisyphean condition, named after the Greek king condemned to roll a stone uphill forever, the experimenter took each finished figure and dismantled it in front of the builder, then handed back the pieces to build again.

The pay was identical. Yet people in the meaningful condition built about eleven figures on average, while those who saw their work destroyed stopped after about seven. Interestingly, among people whose work was kept, those who said they loved Legos built more, but this link almost vanished when the work was taken apart. Seeing the result of their effort mattered for how long people persisted.
lesson: Even modest work feels worth doing when people see it count. Do not let your team's results vanish without a trace: show them what their work became.
people: Dan Ariely, Emir Kamenica, Drazen Prelec
source: Ariely, D., Kamenica, E., and Prelec, D. (2008). Man's search for meaning: The case of Legos. Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, 67(3-4), 671-677.
